extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of experimental science
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on making, recording, and interpreting scientific observations and experiments, with emphasis on detecting, classifying, and managing errors (including constant errors, divergent results, instrument limits, and computational methods such as least squares).

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat divergent results with care; do not arbitrarily exclude them
rubrics_metrics.description: The mere fact of divergence ought not to be taken as conclusive against a result; arbitrary exclusion opens the way to bias and 'cooking' of figures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A divergent number may be the true one or a valuable exception that overturns false theories. To establish its position requires further research; meanwhile give it some weight in mean conclusions and bear the discrepancy in mind. Only when there is reason to suspect considerable bias is rejection the only safe course.

rubrics_metrics.name: Project apparent errors into a curve to inspect their distribution
rubrics_metrics.description: When observations are sufficiently numerous, project the apparent errors into a curve and observe whether it exhibits the symmetrical and characteristic form of the curve of error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the curve is symmetric and characteristic, infer errors arise from many minute independent sources that compensate in the mean. Any considerable irregularity indicates one-sided or large causes of error that should be investigated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Least Squares for estimating multiple unknowns
rubrics_metrics.description: When two or more unknown quantities are involved and cannot be separately determined by simple means, obtain their most probable values by the Method of Least Squares.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reduce many observation-equations to mean equations by multiplying coefficients and summing (forming sums of like terms), then solve these mean equations by ordinary algebra to get most probable values. For practical work, excessive decimal accuracy is unnecessary and decimals may be cut to save computation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Means cannot remove constant (systematic) errors
rubrics_metrics.description: The Method of Means is absolutely incapable of eliminating any error which is always the same, or which always lies in one direction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The observer must carefully remove causes of constant errors. Changing the arrangement or devising entirely different methods of measurement is necessary to detect and correct fixed errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vary apparatus and experimental methods to detect latent/constant errors
rubrics_metrics.description: After making determinations with a certain apparatus or method, alter the arrangement or use different methods to reduce the probability that the same error affects all results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using multiple different methods increases the chance that errors will be balanced or compensate in the mean. Historical examples: Baily's repetition of Cavendish experiments (many series) and Regnault's arbitrary changes to apparatus. If results remain unchanged after modification, errors are probably small, but future generations may still detect overlooked sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use multiple instruments or different parts of an instrument to average out division errors
rubrics_metrics.description: To avoid repeated use of the same mark or part of a divided circle (or equivalent), use different parts or multiple instruments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If each measurement uses a different mark or part, errors of division that are not uniformly directed will tend to cancel in the average; using more than one divided circle is even better.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employ impartial assistants unaware of expected results for routine measurement and computation
rubrics_metrics.description: When extensive numerical series are required, have the numerical work executed by assistants who are not interested in and perhaps unaware of the expected results so that records are rendered perfectly impartial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It may be desirable that routine measurers lack sufficient skill to falsify results without detection. Examples: French logarithm table compiled by many computers under direction; Indian Ordnance Survey measurers selected to prevent undetectable falsification. However, non-routine work still requires skilled, theory-directed observation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observers must combine theoretical expectation with candour and openness
rubrics_metrics.description: Successful investigators must have clear notions of expected results (and confidence in their theories) but also the candour and flexibility to accept unfavorable results and abandon mistaken views.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where work is not routine, assistants cannot replace mind-directed observation; the investigator's attention guided by theory is necessary to notice important points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish observation (passive) from experiment (active); both are sources of experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Observation notes phenomena occurring in the ordinary course of nature; experiment changes conditions by intervention and produces unusual combinations of phenomena.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There are insensible gradations from pure observation to determinate experiment. Many observational sciences can be made experimental by varying times, places, or points of observation (e.g., astronomical selection of times/places, meteorology via balloon ascents).

rubrics_metrics.name: Be aware of sensory and instrumental limits; use appropriate instruments for non-visible phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: Every observation uses one or more senses and is limited by their power; many phenomena escape direct sense-perception and require instruments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Substitute instruments (thermometers, thermopiles, microscopes, telescopes) where senses fail; be conscious of spectral limits (infrared, ultraviolet), auditory limits, and optical resolution limits (diffraction/wavelength limiting microscope resolution). Tailor instruments/conditions (temperature, pressure, vacuum) to mimic or explore conditions beyond ordinary experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for external observational selection effects when inferring frequencies or existence
rubrics_metrics.description: Before drawing inferences from recorded facts, ascertain external conditions under which facts were noticed; the numbers of objects coming to notice may differ from numbers existing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adjust for observational biases and limited observational sphere (example: apparent predominance of elliptic comets is partly due to observational selection). Use probabilistic reasoning to estimate true proportions and abundances (e.g., meteors/comets statistics).

rubrics_metrics.name: When historical records are unreliable, seek verification via new observations or independent records
rubrics_metrics.description: Statements of past events are often made by observers of unknown capacity and impartiality, so they should be replaced by new appeals to nature where possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For past events (eclipses, earthquakes, migrations, extinct animals, customs) use existing statements when necessary but verify by comparing independent records or traditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: When human vigilance is exhausted, rely on the theory of probability
rubrics_metrics.description: After exhausting human precautions (varying methods, instruments, and vigilance), trust probabilistic reasoning to assess and balance remaining errors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using several independent methods increases the probability that errors will not all lie in the same direction; probability theory then justifies interpreting averaged results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classify and discuss results across varied series to disclose differences and corrections
rubrics_metrics.description: When performing many experiments or series, carefully classify and discuss results to disclose the utmost differences and discover necessary corrections (e.g., corrections for air resistance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Baily performed many series and classified 2153 experiments to detect differences; pendulum experiments using many forms determined corrections for air resistance relevant to standards of length.
